transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-01-10
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Arjun Patel (Redwood SE), Elena Ruiz (TideWave VP Product), Samir Qureshi (TideWave ML Platform), Priya Nair (TideWave Security)

-- Auto summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete) --
Redwood demo showing JSON mode and runtime guardrails. Discussion about on-prem/private vs hosted. Security and encryption questions. Agreed next steps for pilot SOW and security artefacts.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, this is Maya from Redwood, thanks for making the time. quick intro, arjun is our solutions engineer, he'll drive the walkthrough. Elena, Samir, Priya, thanks for joining.
[00:15] Elena: Thanks Maya, excited — we booked this to see how typed outputs and tool calls would fit into our billing workflow.
[00:24] Arjun: Cool. Quick agenda — API + Console demo of JSON mode, then runtime patterns (fallbacks, typed responses), and last 15 min Q&A on security and deployment fit. Sound good?
[00:32] Samir: Sounds great, we have about a 45 minute window. we also want to probe latency vs cost tradeoffs, because our SLAs are strict.
[00:40] Maya: Noted. To set context, what's your stack — are you mostly on k8s EKS, or do you run some on-prem?
[00:48] Elena: We're hybrid. Prod inference runs in GCP for most services, but some regulated workloads go to a private cluster in our colo. We use HashiVault and GCP KMS, and SSO via Okta.
[01:05] Priya: Security items: SOC2 is table stakes for us, we need audit logs, key separation, and option for customer-managed keys (HSM/KMS). Also RBAC for console access.
[01:18] Arjun: All common. Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and on-prem package; RBAC and audit logs are in the Console — I'll show screenshots.
[01:26] Maya: Great, jumping into the demo — Arjun?

[01:30] Arjun: Share screen — this is Redwood Console. Quick note, the demo tenant here has a test model pinned to a quantized variant. I'll switch to 'JSON mode' on this endpoint.
[01:45] (screen share)
[01:50] Arjun: JSON mode enforces a response schema — you can upload a JSON Schema or an OpenAPI snippet. When the model replies, the runtime validates and either accepts, coerces, or routes to a fallback. so you get typed objects back.
[02:11] Elena: When you say fallback, do you mean you can call an external service if the model can't generate the structure?
[02:18] Arjun: Exactly. We have a function/tool calling layer — the model can return a 'tool call' object and the runtime will execute it against a configured integration (internal API, database, or a serverless function). If that fails, Redwood can route to a simpler model or return a structured error.
[02:36] Samir: Is the tool execution synchronous? how do you handle long-running ops?
[02:42] Arjun: There are a few patterns. For long ops we surface an async handle and publish status in the Console. For short API calls we do sync. There's also a circuit-breaker with a timeout and retry policy you can tune. we call those guardrails.
[02:58] Priya: Does the runtime log tool inputs/outputs? we need auditability but also PII redaction.
[03:04] Arjun: Yes, logs can be configured to redact fields based on schema paths. You can also set retention and export audit logs to your SIEM.

[03:20] (demo continues: Arjun pastes a schema)
[03:25] Arjun: here's a sample order schema — note required fields, string enums, and nested objects. I'll run a prompt that should produce an order object and a tool call to our 'billing' endpoint.
[03:40] (model completes with small mismatch)
[03:44] Arjun: you'll see the runtime caught a schema mismatch — it flagged a numeric field as string. it auto-coerced in this tenant; in your production you can set it to reject and route to fallback.
[03:56] Elena: Hmm ok, that coercion might be dangerous for us; we prefer strict enforcement for payments.
[04:02] Arjun: Totally. Policy can be strict: reject on mismatch and surface a structured error object to the app. Or, you can run a canary with coercion and logs enabled to evaluate.

[04:20] Maya: Can you show the function calling wiring — how does Redwood authenticate to our internal API?
[04:27] Arjun: We support mTLS, token-based secrets that live in customer vaults, or for Private deployments you can run service connectors inside your VPC. For cloud-hosted endpoints we can store secrets in our encrypted store, but customers often use KMS/HSM with envelope encryption.
[04:45] Samir: So for our colo workloads we'd likely use Private with HSM. What's the maintenance overhead?
[04:52] Arjun: The Private package is delivered with a lightweight control plane and a node group. Redwood handles runtime updates but you control network and keys. Maintenance is similar to a managed k8s add-on — we provide automated upgrades and docs.

[05:10] (timestamp jump; discussion of Optimize recommendations)
[05:12] Arjun: Switching to Redwood Optimize — this module suggests batching, quantization profiles per model, and cache rules. For example, for high-cardinality prompts we recommend prefix KV caching turned off, but for chat histories we enable KV cache to save tokens.
[05:30] Maya: Customers often ask: does Optimize produce one-click configs or just recommendations?
[05:34] Arjun: Today it provides recommended config and an export that can be applied via the Console or API; one-click apply in Dedicated tenants is on roadmap.

[05:50] (demo: showing routing policies)
[05:55] Arjun: Here's smart routing — you can route by latency SLO, cost threshold, or region. And we can set fallbacks like: if the selected model is overloaded, route to a cheaper quantized model or to Dedicated capacity.
[06:10] Samir: Any metrics on cold-start/prefix behaviors?
[06:13] Arjun: We instrument token latency at the model kernel level; you'll see a per-request trace. Cold KV-cache fill will show as a spike. We also provide guidance on warmup traffic for new rollouts.

[06:35] Elena: Ok this looks promising. A couple of security specifics: 1) can we require SAML SSO + SCIM for user provisioning? 2) can Colo hosts use customer-managed KMS?
[06:46] Arjun: Yes and yes. We support SAML/Okta and SCIM for user provisioning. Private supports customer KMS with HSM integrations. I'll attach the SOC2 and architecture diagram after the call.

[07:05] (transcription shows occasional auto-errors)
[07:07] Speaker 1: (mumbles) our latency SLO is 200-300ms p95 for single-turn generations.
[07:14] Arjun: If your p95 target is 300ms, we'll recommend Dedicated pools for steady high-throughput paths and hosted for bursty traffic. The runtime can also route lower-cost batches to quantized models when latency allows.

[07:40] Elena: About observability — can we get token-level billing and per-route charts?
[07:45] Maya: Yes, the Console has token-level cost breakdowns, per-route latency and model traces. We can export to your Datadog or Prometheus.

[08:03] Samir: Are there built-in evals to detect quality regressions after quantization? we can't let hallucinations rise after a model swap.
[08:11] Arjun: Redwood Optimize includes eval monitoring against prompt sets; you can set regression alerts and auto-roll back a rollout if quality drops beyond thresholds. We also support canary traffic split.

[08:40] (demo: function call example)
[08:45] Arjun: Here's an example where the model returns {"tool_call": {"name": "get_customer_balance", "args": {"cust_id": "1234"}}}. The runtime maps that to an integration and calls your accounting API. result is then injected back into the structured response.
[09:02] Priya: We need policy around PII — is there a way to redact before logs leave the runtime?
[09:09] Arjun: Yes, redact at ingestion using schema paths. There are also token scrubbing rules so sensitive fields never hit persisted logs.

[09:30] Elena: What about rate limits and quotas — can we set per-route quotas for different teams?
[09:36] Maya: Yep, per-route quotas, token caps, and overage alerts are configurable. For Dedicated you can also set strict tenancy and burst controls.

[09:50] (the demo runs through a couple of failure scenarios)
[09:55] Arjun: Now I'll simulate the external billing API failing — you'll see the runtime detects the error, marks the tool call failed, and triggers fallback flow to a cached balance or a cheaper model that returns a stubbed object.
[10:15] (the runtime shows structured error object)
[10:20] Elena: That structured error is helpful — our app can render a specific UI for it.

[10:33] Samir: One operational question: if we pin a model version, how do rollouts and quick rollbacks behave?
[10:39] Arjun: You can pin versions per route, do a canary with X% traffic, and auto rollback on error rate or quality regression. The Console shows rollout state and diffs of config.

[11:00] (discussion of pilot)
[11:05] Maya: Based on what you've said, recommended pilot: 30-day scoped pilot, 200k tokens/day, include 3 routes (billing queries, support summary, and order ingestion), run Evaluate harness weekly. Would that match your goals?
[11:18] Elena: Yes that aligns. We'll need the SOW and cost estimate. Also confirm Private vs Hosted — for the billing route we'd prefer Private.
[11:28] Maya: Noted — we'll propose hybrid: Private for billing route, Hosted for support summary for faster iteration.

[11:40] (questions about procurement and timelines)
[11:42] Priya: Procurement will need SOC2 and pen test history. Also a data processing addendum.
[11:50] Maya: We'll attach SOC2, pen test summary, and the DPA.

[12:00] Samir: Any knobs to throttle token cost in the model itself, like response length caps enforced at runtime?
[12:07] Arjun: You can enforce max token outputs per route, or use structured templates to limit verbosity. The runtime can truncate and return a structured 'truncated:true' flag.

[12:25] Elena: Can you demonstrate how a schema evolves? we may add fields later.
[12:31] Arjun: In Console you can upload a new schema version and choose compatibility policy (strict, additive only, or coercive). We also keep a schema history and show which routes depend on which schema.

[12:50] (demo shows schema history; a minor transcription mismatch: 'schema histery')
[12:55] Arjun: (laughs) the auto transcript calls it 'schema histery' sometimes.

[13:05] Priya: One more on encryption — for Hosted can we use customer-managed keys so logs are encrypted under our KMS even in hosted?
[13:14] Arjun: We offer envelope encryption and can integrate with your KMS for key rotation. For full separation we recommend Private.

[13:30] (mid-call recap)
[13:33] Maya: Quick recap: JSON mode with strict schema enforcement available; function calls with mTLS/token or VPC connectors; Optimize suggests configs; pilot SOW proposed hybrid deployment.

[13:50] Elena: Looks good. who will be our primary contact at Redwood during pilot?
[13:54] Maya: I'll be AE contact; Arjun is SE lead for onboarding. We'll also loop in Solutions success during kickoff.

[14:05] (closing Q&A; a couple of small interruptions and side chatter)
[14:10] Samir: do you have any case studies for regulated industries?
[14:14] Maya: Yes — I'll send two short case studies: one healthcare customer on Private and one fintech on Dedicated.
[14:20] Priya: Please include any SOC2 scope specifics — encryption at rest/in transit, key management, and pen test cadence.
[14:26] Maya: Will do.

[14:35] (wrap up)
[14:36] Maya: Ok everybody, thanks — action items: we'll send SOW + security pack + benchmark checklist. TideWave to confirm pilot target and available infra contacts. Any final questions?
[14:47] Elena: None from me. Thanks for the thorough run.
[14:50] Samir: thanks, good session.
[14:53] Priya: Thanks, bye.
[14:55] Maya: Bye everyone, we'll follow up by Thursday.

End of transcript.
